report.source_text: During the subsequent 9 months, visual acuity deteriorated considerably to a Snellen fraction of less than 20/200 on the right side and 25/100 on the left side. Concomitant bilateral cataracts and significant atrophy of the optic nerve (right>left) were documented. Bilateral cataract surgery was performed in a private practice without any amelioration of visual acuity. A tumour or inflammatory alterations of the optic nerve were ruled out by a brain MRI. A genetic panel for >100 genes related to hereditary optic atrophy including Leber’s hereditary optic neuropathy was also unrevealing.

Furthermore, a prominent relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) was found. A repeated MRI scan showed regression of the formerly described herniated disc without any signs of myelopathy. Electrophysiological testing did not show any clear evidence for the presence of a polyneuropathy.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 60-year-old carpenter presented with 3 months of diplopia initially attributed to congenital IVth cranial nerve paresis. On further history, he disclosed a syphilis infection 30 years prior that was likely inadequately treated with an unknown oral antibiotic. Eight months after initial presentation, he developed progressive neurological symptoms including recurrent diplopia, pelvic pain radiating to the right leg, urge incontinence, sensory polyneuropathy in the lower limbs, left VIth cranial nerve palsy, decreased deep tendon reflexes, reduced vibration sense, and unsteady gait. Four years after initial symptoms, he presented with severe gait ataxia from diminished proprioception, absent deep tendon reflexes, Argyll-Robertson pupils (diminished light reflex with preserved convergence), and almost complete vision loss. Subsequently, visual acuity deteriorated further with bilateral cataracts and optic nerve atrophy (right > left); brain MRI ruled out tumour or inflammatory alterations; genetic panel for hereditary optic atrophy was unrevealing. One year later, he had further progression of ataxia with prominent relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD); repeated MRI showed regression of herniated disc without myelopathy; rheumatological screening and tumour markers were unremarkable; electrophysiological testing did not show clear polyneuropathy. This clinical trajectory—characterized by progressive dorsal spinal cord degeneration with sensory ataxia, proprioceptive loss, absent reflexes, Argyll-Robertson pupils, and cranial nerve involvement in the context of remote inadequately treated syphilis—is pathognomonic for tabes dorsalis. The known final diagnosis statement confirms that serological and CSF syphilis activity was documented.
